title: Anatomy and Physiology of Slaughter Stock

lessons.title: Body structure and the carcass
lessons.html:
Knowing normal before finding abnormal

A meat examiner can only recognise disease if they know what normal organs and tissues look, feel and smell like. Slaughter stock in South Africa are mainly cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, and sometimes horses or game where approved.

Directional terms

TermMeaning
Cranial / caudalTowards the head / towards the tail
Dorsal / ventralTowards the back / towards the belly
Medial / lateralTowards the midline / away from the midline
Proximal / distalCloser to / further from the body on a limb

Skeleton and muscle

The skeleton gives structure: skull, vertebral column (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and tail vertebrae), ribs, sternum, pelvis and limb bones. Major carcass cuts follow the skeleton. Muscle is the meat; fat lies under the skin (subcutaneous), between muscles (intermuscular), within muscles (marbling) and around organs such as the kidneys.

Body cavities

  • Thoracic cavity (chest): heart, lungs, oesophagus, trachea; lined by the pleura.
  • Abdominal cavity: stomach(s), intestines, liver, spleen, kidneys; lined by the peritoneum.
  • Pelvic cavity: bladder, rectum, reproductive organs.

The diaphragm separates chest and abdomen.

Lymphatic system

Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped organs that filter lymph fluid draining from tissues. They react to infection by enlarging, becoming wet, reddened or containing pus or calcified lesions. During inspection, specific lymph nodes are examined and cut because they show what is happening in the area they drain. Learn the location of the main nodes of the head, lungs, liver, intestines and carcass for each species, as set out in the inspection procedures.

lessons.title: Organ systems of slaughter animals
lessons.html:
Organs the examiner inspects

Digestive system

Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have four stomach compartments: rumen (large fermentation vat), reticulum (honeycomb lining, where swallowed wire and nails can lodge), omasum (many leaf-like folds) and abomasum (true glandular stomach). Pigs and horses have a simple stomach. The liver, the largest gland, lies against the diaphragm; it stores nutrients, detoxifies and produces bile. Cattle and sheep have a gall bladder; horses do not.

Respiratory system

Air passes through the nostrils, larynx and trachea to the lungs. Healthy lungs are pink, spongy, light and float in water. Lungs are divided into lobes, and the number of lobes differs slightly between species.

Circulatory system

The heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles. The left ventricle wall is thicker because it pumps blood around the body. The heart sits in the pericardial sac. Blood vessels carry blood away from (arteries) and back to (veins) the heart.

Urinary system

Two kidneys filter blood to form urine. Cattle kidneys are lobulated (divided into lobes); sheep and pig kidneys are smooth and bean-shaped. Kidneys are surrounded by kidney fat.

Spleen

The spleen stores and filters blood and contains immune tissue. Enlargement can indicate disease, for example anthrax in cattle (when a suspected anthrax carcass must not be opened).

Reproductive and endocrine organs

Ovaries, uterus, testes and udder are examined for abnormalities such as mastitis or pregnancy. Glands such as the thyroid and adrenals produce hormones.

Physiology after slaughter

After bleeding, muscle continues to use glycogen without oxygen, producing lactic acid. The pH falls and rigor mortis sets in. Stress before slaughter alters this, causing meat defects.

Key points

  • Know normal anatomy to recognise abnormal findings.
  • The diaphragm separates thoracic and abdominal cavities.
  • Lymph nodes show what is happening in the area they drain.
  • Ruminants have rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.
  • Healthy lungs are pink and spongy; cattle kidneys are lobulated.
